title: Output Caching in ASP.NET Core
description: Use the ASP.NET Core output caching middleware to cache entire endpoint outputs with fine-grained policies, vary-by rules, and cache eviction controls.

data.text: Output caching was introduced in ASP.NET Core 7.0 as a more powerful successor to response caching. While response caching relies on HTTP headers and works at the edge, output caching operates inside the ASP.NET Core pipeline with full programmatic control. You can define cache policies using attributes, fluent configuration, or the new OutputCacheOptions API, and control eviction, locking, and varying without relying on client headers.

Output caching is not just for HTML pages — it works with any endpoint type including minimal APIs, controllers, and gRPC. It integrates with IDistributedCache for distributed scenarios, so cached outputs are shared across server instances.

terms.definition: A policy object that defines how an endpoint's output should be cached: duration, vary-by rules, expiration modes, and eviction triggers.
The central options class where named policies are registered and retrieved by the middleware.
Rules that create separate cache entries for different header values, query keys, route values, or custom claims.
A mechanism that serializes requests for the same cache key while the first request regenerates the value, preventing duplicate work.

data.title: Cache Locking Prevents Stampedes
data.text: When a cached entry expires, multiple concurrent requests can all try to regenerate it simultaneously. Enable locking to ensure only one request rebuilds the cache while others wait for the result.

data.caption: Output caching middleware pipeline flow
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Incoming Request] --> B[OutputCache Middleware]
    B --> C{Entry in Cache?}
    C -->|Hit| D[Return Cached Output]
    C -->|Miss| E{Lock Held?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Wait for Lock Release]
    E -->|No| G[Acquire Lock]
    G --> H[Invoke Next Middleware]
    H --> I[Capture Response]
    I --> J[Store in Cache]
    J --> K[Release Lock]
    K --> L[Return Response to Client]
    F --> L
    D --> L

data.text: Output cache entries can be evicted in three ways: by expiration, by explicit eviction via IOutputCacheEntryEvictor, or by triggering a tag-based group eviction. You can resolve an IOutputCacheEntryEvictor from DI and call EvictByTagAsync to invalidate a set of cached endpoints whenever related data changes.

data.title: Evicting Cache by Tag
data.content: Inject the evictor and clear cached product pages when a product is updated.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Output caching operates inside the ASP.NET Core pipeline with full programmatic control
Named policies defined in OutputCacheOptions are reusable across endpoints
VaryBy rules create separate cache entries for different request dimensions
Cache locking prevents stampedes when entries expire and are regenerated
IOutputCacheEntryEvictor enables tag-based eviction from within your application code
data.takeaway: Output caching is the preferred server-side caching approach in modern ASP.NET Core applications.
